title: Practically efficient post-quantum indistinguishability obfuscation

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a practical compiler that transforms ordinary classical programs into obfuscated programs, preserves their behavior, and provides indistinguishability obfuscation (iO) security against quantum adversaries. In plain language, if two circuits compute the same function and satisfy the formal size conditions, their obfuscated versions should be computationally indistinguishable. This is an equivalence-based protection: it does not promise to conceal everything about a program or anything its outputs reveal. This explanation synthesizes the concept and formal distinctions supplied in the review.

The target covers general polynomial-size circuits rather than only a restricted family such as point functions. Classical general-circuit feasibility has been established conditionally on specified hardness assumptions, but the supplied post-quantum research identifies a separate challenge in obtaining credible quantum-resistant foundations. The innovation requires those foundations and usable implementation costs together; neither a feasibility theorem nor a new assumption alone delivers the complete capability.

Scope synthesis: the programs being obfuscated are classical, while the adversary may use quantum computation. Obfuscating quantum programs is a separate target. Constructions from established assumptions and constructions from a new assumption belong within this entry when they deliver the same practical, general-circuit, post-quantum capability.

significance.text: A usable realization would make a powerful theoretical cryptographic tool available for deployed systems. Lin's 2021 invited-talk abstract documents broad consequences of iO, including functional encryption, fully homomorphic encryption, multiparty non-interactive key exchange, and succinct garbled random access machines. These consequences support the innovation's potential importance, but they do not establish that every derived application would inherit practical performance or post-quantum security without additional assumptions, proofs, and engineering.

Conditional impact synthesis: practical post-quantum iO could support distributing useful programs with application-specific proofs that protect embedded information while allowing execution without a trusted device. The secrecy argument must be established for each application. An embedded secret that the program reveals through its behavior remains exposed, and the iO guarantee alone does not provide arbitrary secret protection, tamper resistance, or copy prevention.

The relevant limit is the impossibility of general virtual-black-box obfuscation: the ambition that an obfuscated program reveal no more than access to its input-output behavior cannot be met for every program family. The 2001 work establishes an unobfuscatable family under weak formulations of that intuition. It does not rule out every restricted-function obfuscator, and it does not eliminate the distinct iO target. The supplied review relies on the readable abstract for this distinction because the retained PDF extraction was garbled and truncated.

missing_breakthrough.text: The scientific gap is a convincing foundation for general-circuit iO secure against quantum adversaries. Hsieh, Jain, and Lin describe earlier lattice-inspired approaches using new LWE-with-hints assumptions and report structural vulnerabilities discovered through subsequent cryptanalysis. Their Circular Security with Random Opening assumption, abbreviated CRO, supplies a new candidate foundation. Their assessment that it appears resistant to known techniques is a reason for further investigation, rather than evidence that its long-term security is established.

The classical theorem does not close that gap. Lin's 2021 abstract states a construction from subexponential hardness assumptions involving learning parity with noise over prime fields with specified noise parameters, a Boolean constant-locality pseudorandom generator with polynomial stretch, and Decision Linear on symmetric bilinear groups. These qualifications matter: the result is conditional on a particular collection of strong hardness hypotheses, and it does not establish the proposed practical post-quantum capability.

Engineering synthesis: a successful construction must also make obfuscation, storage, and evaluation affordable at a stated security level. This requires concrete parameter choices, manageable circuit expansion, usable compilation time and memory, and evaluation costs that remain acceptable on meaningful programs. Asymptotic polynomial time alone does not answer those questions. The supplied evidence contains no verified measurements from which to identify the dominant practical bottleneck or predict when it will be overcome.

Foundational progress must avoid assuming a substantial part of the desired capability. Branco, Jain, and Srinivasan's supplied abstract describes a standard-model result that assumes post-quantum average-case iO in addition to LWE. That conditional relationship may clarify which obfuscation tasks suffice, but it does not establish post-quantum iO from LWE alone.

current_state.text: Classical general-circuit feasibility is supported by Lin's FSTTCS 2021 invited-talk abstract, reporting joint work with Aayush Jain and Amit Sahai. Its theorem concludes subexponentially secure iO for all polynomial-size circuits under the three specified subexponential-hardness assumptions. The retained document is a one-page abstract containing the theorem statement, rather than the full construction and proof. It supports the conditional feasibility result but does not establish the construction's recursive architecture or practical resource requirements.

The research attributes a large-polynomial complexity statement and an open practical-efficiency question to Jain, Lin, and Sahai's 2024 Communications of the ACM article. However, no artifact of that article was retained in the supplied source packet, so the review could not verify those passages. They remain unverified source attributions here, rather than established measurements or a demonstrated inability to execute every relevant construction.

Hsieh, Jain, and Lin's ePrint 2025/390, recorded in the research as received on March 1, 2025, proposes lattice-based post-quantum iO from CRO. The retained landing-page abstract reports attacks on earlier assumptions and says the new assumption does not appear vulnerable to known cryptanalytic techniques. This is a proposed foundation reported by its authors. The supplied evidence does not independently verify all preceding attacks, establish CRO's durability under later scrutiny, or provide implementation benchmarks.

Branco, Jain, and Srinivasan's ePrint 2025/2215, identified in the research as a TCC 2025 paper, has a landing-page revision dated May 28, 2026. Its abstract explicitly describes the existence of post-quantum iO as an open question and notes that lattice candidates use new, non-standard assumptions, many of which have been broken. Its conditional standard-model result retains a post-quantum average-case iO assumption alongside LWE. Consequently, this paper is evidence of an ongoing foundational question at that revision, rather than an unconditional resolution.

Evidence-bound synthesis: none of the readable retained texts reports a runnable general-purpose obfuscator with the proposed practical post-quantum guarantees. Most of the relevant evidence consists of abstracts or landing pages, so that observation cannot establish absence from the complete papers or the wider literature. The supplied freshness record is empty; subsequent developments through November 1, 2026 remain unassessed. The packet therefore does not demonstrate completion of this innovation, while also not proving that no later or unexamined result exists.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: publish an executable implementation of a general-circuit iO construction and evaluate it on a disclosed, nontrivial benchmark suite containing circuits of at least 2^16 gates. At a stated security parameter, demonstrate obfuscated size and evaluation time within 100 times those of matched original implementations. These numerical thresholds are proposed milestones for this record, not established community standards or reported achievements.
completion_criteria.label: General-circuit obfuscation achieves ≤100× size and evaluation time on ≥2^16-gate benchmarks

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements: release implementation code, circuit representations, benchmark inputs, parameter choices, hardware specifications, timing methods, and the baseline implementations used for comparison. Report obfuscation time, peak memory, output size, and evaluation time separately, including any preprocessing or amortization. Independent teams should be able to reproduce correctness and overhead measurements and identify workloads on which the implementation becomes impractical.
completion_criteria.label: Released artifacts enable independent reproduction of correctness and full resource costs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed security requirements: provide a general-circuit correctness and security argument, with a reduction against quantum adversaries under explicitly stated assumptions. Disclose the security losses and their consequences for concrete parameters. Record a defined period of public cryptanalysis, a cutoff date, and any known attacks or parameter restrictions. Having no known break at that cutoff would be evidence of scrutiny, not proof that an assumption will remain secure.
completion_criteria.label: General-circuit quantum security reductions disclose assumptions, losses, and public cryptanalysis

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: point-function-only obfuscation and an asymptotic construction that cannot be executed on the disclosed workloads would not satisfy this milestone. Finite benchmarks establish demonstrated breadth and costs for those workloads; they cannot establish literal universality or replace a general-circuit security theorem. Claims about a derived application, including protection of an embedded secret, would require their own proofs and performance evaluations.
completion_criteria.label: General-circuit obfuscation executes disclosed workloads with explicitly bounded benchmark claims

related_concepts.text: Roster synthesis — CRY-01, A proof that an explicit one-way function exists, and CRY-02, Public-key encryption from one-way functions: these entries concern foundational existence and implication questions. CRY-03 instead seeks a stronger program-transformation capability with practical costs and quantum-adversary security. A conditional obfuscation construction does not prove an explicit one-way function secure without assumptions, nor does it resolve whether one-way functions alone suffice for public-key encryption.

Roster synthesis — CRY-04, General-purpose private computation at near-plaintext cost: both entries seek practical access to powerful cryptographic computation. Private computation emphasizes protecting data during computation; CRY-03 emphasizes indistinguishability of implementations of equivalent programs. The documented iO consequences include fully homomorphic and functional encryption, which provide a theoretical connection, but practical iO would not by itself establish near-plaintext costs for private computation.

Roster synthesis — CRY-05, Publicly verifiable unclonable money and copy-protected programs: the overlap is protection of computational artifacts, but the guarantees differ. CRY-03 targets classical software secure against quantum analysis. It does not make that software physically unclonable, prevent copying its bits, or establish the quantum-state guarantees relevant to unclonable money and quantum copy protection.

Roster synthesis — CRY-06, Practical classical verification of quantum computation, and CRY-07, Position verification that works in physical spacetime: these address different trust questions. CRY-06 concerns checking quantum computations through classical verification; CRY-07 concerns establishing location under physical and adversarial constraints. Resistance to quantum attacks on an obfuscated classical program supplies neither guarantee.

Roster synthesis — CRY-08, Metadata-private messaging at ordinary cost, and CRY-09, Post-quantum timed release with a sequentiality theorem: these share the demand for meaningful security at usable cost. Metadata privacy requires system-level protection of communication patterns, while timed release requires a defensible delay or sequentiality guarantee. Obfuscation might become a component of particular designs, but the supplied evidence establishes no construction that resolves either target.

Roster synthesis — CRY-10, A conclusive quantum classification of deployed lattice encryption: this entry overlaps with scrutiny of lattice assumptions but has a different scope. Classifying deployed lattice encryption would not automatically validate the specialized hints, circular-security conditions, or other assumptions used by a post-quantum iO candidate. Conversely, progress on those specialized assumptions would not settle the security classification of deployed lattice encryption.

brief.title: Software that hides its workings from quantum computers
possible: Developers could distribute ordinary software in a form that still runs correctly but conceals how it was written. Even someone using a quantum computer could not reliably distinguish protected versions of programs that do the same thing and meet matching size conditions.
why: This could let people run useful software that protects embedded information without relying on a trusted device. It would also give developers a foundation for encryption that allows computation on protected data.

sources.showed: They proved that some program families cannot be protected under a guarantee that reveals nothing beyond their input-output behavior.
sources.cited_for: It explains why hiding everything about every program is an impossible goal.
sources.not_established: This impossibility result does not rule out protection based on indistinguishability between equivalent programs.

sources.who: Aayush Jain, Huijia Lin and Amit Sahai
sources.showed: This research article discusses a construction for hiding program implementations under stated mathematical assumptions and the question of practical efficiency.
sources.cited_for: It addresses the gap between theoretical feasibility and practical efficiency.
sources.not_established: A theoretical construction does not establish affordable execution costs or security against quantum attackers.

sources.who: Pedro Branco, Abhishek Jain and Akshayaram Srinivasan
sources.showed: They showed how quantum-resistant protection for general programs can follow from assumptions that include protection for a narrower class of functions.
sources.quote: We construct (post-quantum) i$\mathcal{O}$ for general circuits in the standard model based on (post-quantum) sub-exponentially secure LWE and (post-quantum) sub-exponentially secure {\em average-case} i$\mathcal{O}$
sources.cited_for: Protecting a narrower class of functions can suffice as a foundation for protecting general programs.
sources.not_established: The result still assumes a form of the desired protection and does not demonstrate practical costs.

sources.who: Yao-Ching Hsieh, Aayush Jain and Huijia Lin
sources.showed: In a preprint, they proposed a new mathematical security assumption for quantum-resistant program protection. They showed how its structure avoids classes of attacks against earlier proposals.
sources.quote: These two features--- marginally random hints and the absence of (natural) noise leakage---rule out important classes of attacks that had undermined all previous LWE-with-hint assumptions for iO.
sources.cited_for: It offers a candidate foundation designed to avoid weaknesses in earlier assumptions.
sources.not_established: Avoiding known attacks does not establish lasting security under independent scrutiny or practical implementation costs.

sources.who: Huijia Lin, Aayush Jain and Amit Sahai
sources.showed: They proved that general programs can receive equivalence-based protection if specified mathematical problems are sufficiently hard.
sources.quote: In this work, we show how to construct indistinguishability obfuscation from the subexponential hardness of three well-founded assumptions.
sources.cited_for: It establishes conditional theoretical feasibility for general programs against classical attackers.
sources.not_established: The theorem does not establish quantum resistance or usable compilation, storage and execution costs.

shown: Huijia Lin, Aayush Jain and Amit Sahai established theoretical protection for general programs under specified hardness assumptions. Hsieh, Jain and Lin proposed a quantum-resistant foundation in a preprint. These are theoretical advances; practical quantum-resistant protection remains a target.
missing: A convincing mathematical foundation for general program protection against quantum attackers remains needed.
An executable implementation must demonstrate affordable compilation, memory, storage and execution costs.
Independent teams must reproduce correct behavior and the full resource measurements.
Applications that protect embedded secrets need their own security proofs and performance measurements.

milestones.explanation: An executable implementation would have to keep size and execution time within 100 times matched originals on the specified large benchmarks at a stated security level. This would establish a concrete efficiency result.

milestones.explanation: Released code, inputs, parameters and measurement details would have to let independent teams reproduce correctness and all resource costs, including preparation. This would expose costs hidden by selective reporting.

milestones.explanation: A proof for general programs would have to state assumptions and security losses, alongside a defined period of public attack analysis and known restrictions. This would make the security claim assessable.

milestones.explanation: The construction would have to execute the disclosed workloads beyond narrowly restricted functions, with claims bounded by those tests. This would establish demonstrated scope; application claims would need separate proofs and tests.

page.title: Post-quantum indistinguishability obfuscation
page.definition: A classical compiler converts Boolean circuits, programs built from logical gates, into equivalent executable code with measured costs. For all polynomial-size circuits, obfuscations of equal-size circuits computing the same function are indistinguishable to quantum polynomial-time attackers, with advantage smaller than every inverse polynomial in a security parameter.

goal.need: For an n-input Boolean circuit, its complete truth table has 2^n entries. Polynomial-time iO avoids that exponential representation. Its uses include fully homomorphic encryption, functional encryption, multiparty non-interactive key exchange and succinct garbled random-access machines. Quantum resistance is a separate requirement: the 2022 Jain–Lin–Sahai survey states that a quantum computer breaks their bilinear-map construction in polynomial time.

statements.body: Jain–Lin–Sahai research team, ICM 2022 invited contribution
statements.quote: in a way that the resulting scheme yields concrete implementable efficiency?
statements.context: The developers ask whether their approach, or another construction, can achieve concrete efficiency.

statements.body: Jain–Lin–Sahai research team, ICM 2022 invited contribution
statements.quote: build iO on any combination of well-studied postquantum assumptions
statements.context: The developers identify post-quantum security as a separate open problem.

statements.quote: The main pressing question in this area is whether post-quantum i$\mathcal{O}$ exists.

completion.title: An independent team reproduces an executable general-circuit post-quantum iO compiler.
completion.criterion: An executable classical compiler for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits has peer-reviewed correctness and quantum-security proofs under explicit hardness assumptions. An independent team reproduces compilation and correct evaluation of disclosed programs at concrete parameters, including the reduction's quantum-security bound and measured compilation time, peak memory, output size and evaluation time. The executable implements the proved construction. Finite benchmarks establish execution costs for those programs; the theorem establishes generality and security.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no external acceptance test combining general circuits, quantum security and concrete implementation efficiency was found.
completion.basis: Searches of DARPA SafeWare, NIST material, prize criteria, iO definitions and implementation papers found no combined acceptance test or numerical practicality cutoff. This minimum test combines the published post-quantum security definition with the developers' concrete-efficiency goal and independent replication. It establishes executable feasibility; it does not establish an externally defined level of practical efficiency.

milestones.title: An implementation of an iO candidate produces and evaluates an obfuscated program.
milestones.criterion: A software implementation of a candidate iO construction produces an obfuscated program that executes with the original input-output behavior. Apon and colleagues report an implementation in a preprint received on 5 October 2014. This is implementation evidence for a candidate construction, without a post-quantum security claim; it is not evidence that general-circuit iO security was experimentally established.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback: implementation papers provide prototype demonstrations, but no accepted minimum workload or resource threshold for an initial demonstration was found.

milestones.title: A polynomial-time construction provides conditional classical iO security for all polynomial-size circuits.
milestones.criterion: A polynomial-time obfuscator preserves outputs with probability 1 and makes obfuscations of equal-size equivalent circuits computationally indistinguishable. Lin's theorem supplies this conditionally on subexponential hardness of learning parity with noise over prime fields, with error rate k^(-δ), δ>0; a constant-locality Boolean pseudorandom generator stretching n bits to n^(1+τ), τ>0; and Decision Linear in symmetric prime-order bilinear groups. The theorem covers all polynomial-size circuits. The bilinear-group construction does not provide quantum resistance.
milestones.set_by: Cryptographic community's iO definition; the general-circuit threshold is stated in Lin's FSTTCS 2021 theorem.
milestones.threshold_quote: Then, (subexponentially secure) indistinguishability obfuscation for all polynomial-size circuits exist.

milestones.title: A general-circuit iO construction has negligible distinguishing advantage against quantum attackers.
milestones.criterion: A classical polynomial-time compiler preserves outputs with probability 1. For every equal-size equivalent circuit pair and quantum polynomial-time distinguisher D, |Pr[D(O(C0))=1]−Pr[D(O(C1))=1]| is negligible in λ: eventually below λ^(-c) for every c>0. Hsieh, Jain and Lin propose a construction under Circular Security with Random Opening, a new lattice assumption; their source is a preprint, not peer reviewed. Branco and colleagues' standard-model reduction additionally assumes post-quantum average-case iO and therefore does not establish iO from learning with errors alone.
milestones.set_by: Cryptographic community's post-quantum iO definition, as used in Bartusek and colleagues, Definition 3.3.

milestones.title: A compiler implementing a post-quantum general-circuit iO construction executes disclosed programs.
milestones.criterion: An executable compiler implements a construction with a correctness proof and a security reduction against quantum polynomial-time adversaries. At explicit finite parameters, it completes compilation and evaluation of disclosed programs, producing the original outputs. The demonstration establishes actual compilation time, peak memory, obfuscated size and evaluation time on identified hardware, together with the reduction's concrete security bound. Independent reproduction is reserved for completion.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback: searches of SafeWare, benchmarking papers and post-quantum iO sources found no externally fixed workload or resource threshold for this implementation stage.

not_found: No external test combining general-circuit post-quantum iO security with numerical limits on compilation time, memory, storage and evaluation time was found.
No independently reproduced executable general-circuit post-quantum iO implementation with concrete quantum-security parameters was found.
The CACM article and the full PDFs of ePrint 2014/779, 2025/390 and 2025/2215 could not be opened; their accessible abstracts do not establish full construction details or implementation costs.
No published sequence of implementation stages leading to a shared practical-efficiency threshold was found.

results.finding: A general-circuit post-quantum iO construction is claimed under 2 sub-exponential security assumptions.
results.detail: The standard-model reduction assumes both post-quantum LWE and post-quantum average-case iO. The supplied text does not state the exact correctness and negligible-advantage guarantees required by the criterion.
results.quote: We construct (post-quantum) i$\mathcal{O}$ for general circuits in the standard model based on (post-quantum) sub-exponentially secure LWE and (post-quantum) sub-exponentially secure {\em average-case} i$\mathcal{O}$

results.finding: Proposes post-quantum iO under one new lattice assumption, Circular Security with Random Opening.
results.detail: The supplied abstract describes building iO under CRO but does not state the compiler's correctness, general-circuit scope, or negligible distinguishing bound against quantum attackers.
results.quote: To build iO under this less-structured CRO assumption, we develop several new technical ideas.

results.finding: Lin and colleagues report iO for all polynomial-size circuits under 3 subexponentially hard assumptions.
results.detail: The assumptions are LPN over prime fields, a constant-locality Boolean PRG with polynomial stretch, and Decision Linear in symmetric prime-order bilinear groups. The source does not claim quantum resistance.
results.quote: Then, (subexponentially secure) indistinguishability obfuscation for all polynomial-size circuits exist.

results.finding: Simplified GGH15 obfuscator: sample size not stated; evaluation took under 25 minutes per input.
results.detail: The implementation produced and evaluated obfuscated read-once branching programs. It omitted protection against mixed-input attacks, so the result does not establish general-circuit or post-quantum iO security.

results.finding: Conditional iO construction from bilinear groups and two LPN variants; sample size and numerical result not applicable.
